headline: Cornelius Bassett, enslaver of Rebecca Amos and Nancy Michael, dies; Nancy and family sold to Joseph Allen of Tisbury
text: Cornelius Bassett, the enslaver of Rebecca Amos and her daughter Nancy Michael, died in 1779, after which Nancy, her brother, and likely her mother were sold to Joseph Allen of Tisbury.

headline: Massachusetts effectively bans slavery
text: Slavery was effectively abolished in Massachusetts in 1783, establishing that anyone born in the state thereafter was born free.

headline: Indian Nonintercourse Act enacted, barring sale of Native lands without public treaty
text: The Indian Nonintercourse Act was originally enacted, barring the sale of Native lands to any person or state without a public treaty conducted under United States authority.

headline: Sarah Francis petitions to sell her land
text: Sarah Francis, a Wampanoag woman, petitioned the Massachusetts state in 1811 to sell her land. The petition was granted, marking the start of sustained petitioning by elderly women for land access to support themselves amid economic hardship.

headline: Gay Head receives gubernatorial-appointed guardians
text: Gay Head received gubernatorial-appointed guardians in 1811, beginning a new phase of state oversight of the Wampanoag community.

headline: Gay Head Petition Series: Sustained sequence of petitions to sell communal lands
text: The Gay Head Petition Series of 1811–1824 saw a sustained sequence of petitions to the Massachusetts state legislature to sell lands held in common by the tribe, reshaping elder care and guardianship in the community.

headline: Beulah Occouch and Abraham Cooper petition against the 1811 guardianship act
text: Beulah Occouch, Abraham Cooper, and several other Gay Head residents petitioned the legislature critiquing the 1811 guardianship act, accusing appointed overseers and Native leader Zachariah Howwaswee of being 'unconstitutionally, unlawfully, cruelly, and unjustly' complicit in the community's mistreatment.

headline: Mercy Popenna, Hannah Pocknet, and Bathsheba Wickett petition to sell land for support in old age
text: Mercy Popenna, Hannah Pocknet, and Bathsheba Wickett petitioned to sell land for support in old age, but were met with community protests over the reduction of communal lands.

headline: George Peters leads remonstrance petition against land sales by elderly women
text: On Christmas Day 1823, George Peters of Tisbury drafted a remonstrance petition, signed by Black and Native residents including members of the Peters, Mingo, James, and Weeks families, protesting the Popenna, Pocknet, and Wickett land sales and the reduction of communal lands.

headline: Indian Removal Act passes; William Vanderhoop first visits Gay Head
text: Andrew Jackson's Indian Removal Act was passed in 1830. Around this time, William Vanderhoop, born in Holland of Dutch and Surinamese ancestry, first visited Gay Head aboard a merchant trading vessel and made his home there, later marrying Beulah Occouch Salisbury.

headline: Mashpee Revolt: William Apess leads petition drive and uprising
text: The Mashpee Revolt of 1833 and 1834, led by Pequot Methodist preacher William Apess, grew out of decades of petitioning and signaled a new willingness by the Massachusetts legislature to alter Native guardianship arrangements. The largest petition carried 287 signatures.

headline: Solomon Attaquin chosen as Mashpee selectman; captains the Native of Marshpee
text: Beginning in 1837, Solomon Attaquin, a leader of the Mashpee petition drive, was chosen as a Mashpee selectman. In 1837, he set sail from Mashpee Harbor at Popponesset as captain of the Native of Marshpee, a vessel built and crewed entirely by Mashpee Wampanoag.

headline: Cynthia Conant Attaquin and 13 Wampanoag women petition against railroad discrimination
text: Cynthia Conant Attaquin and thirteen other Wampanoag women of Mashpee petitioned the Massachusetts Senate to prohibit railroad companies from excluding passengers on the basis of color, part of a statewide 1842 campaign that sent sixty petitions with at least 5,129 signatures to the Massachusetts Legislature.

headline: William and Beulah Vanderhoop lead cranberry petition with 75 other Gay Headers
text: William Vanderhoop, Beulah Occouch Salisbury Vanderhoop, and seventy-five other Gay Head petitioners won passage of a petition protecting the community's exclusive access to its cranberry bogs from outside harvesters.

headline: Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 mandates return of runaways from free states
text: The 1850 Fugitive Slave Act mandated that runaway slaves be returned to their enslavers even after reaching a free state like Massachusetts.

headline: Edgartown v. Tisbury: Massachusetts SJC affirms Nancy Michael's freedom
text: In May 1852, the Court of Common Pleas in Dukes County heard Inhabitants of Edgartown v. Inhabitants of Tisbury, ruling that Nancy Michael's daughter Lucy was born free. In October 1852, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court upheld the lower court's ruling with Associate Justice Theron Metcalf writing that Nancy Michael derived no settlement from her enslaved mother or her mother's master.

headline: Randall Burton escapes enslavement via Edgartown Harbor with help from Gay Head women
text: Randall Burton escaped enslavement via Edgartown Harbor on Martha's Vineyard in 1854. In September 1854, news broke that Randall Burton had escaped custody at Holmes Hole after Gay Head women brought him a dress and bonnet and helped disguise him, aiding his escape by boat near Menemsha Bight to safe harbor in New Bedford and onward to freedom.

headline: Massachusetts directs investigation into condition of all Native Indians
text: The Massachusetts Legislature passed the Act of April 6, 1859, directing an investigation into the condition of the Commonwealth's Indians that became the basis for John Milton Earle's commission and report.

headline: John Milton Earle selected as Commissioner of Indian Affairs for Massachusetts
text: In 1860, John Milton Earle was selected as Commissioner of Indian Affairs for Massachusetts, tasked with examining the condition of all Indians and their descendants domiciled in the Commonwealth.

headline: Earle's report recommends automatic enfranchisement but opts-in status for Mashpee and Gay Head
text: John Milton Earle conducted a detailed 1861 study of Massachusetts Indian affairs, recommending automatic enfranchisement for most Native individuals while allowing those in seven communities, including Mashpee, Gay Head, and Herring Pond, to opt in by paying a poll tax.

headline: Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery; Fourteenth Amendment grants citizenship to formerly enslaved
text: In 1865, Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery and the Fourteenth Amendment granting citizenship rights to the formerly enslaved, though 'Indians not taxed' were excluded from citizenship.

headline: Massachusetts Indian Enfranchisement Act dissolves guardianship system entirely
text: By 1869, Massachusetts dissolved the Native guardianship system entirely, extending citizenship to all remaining Native individuals and shifting responsibility for indigent care to the Board of State Charities. The Indian Enfranchisement Act of 1869 extended voting rights to Indigenous communities across the state, except Mashpee and Gay Head, while dispersing communal tribal lands among individual landholders.

headline: Legislative committee meets in Mashpee meetinghouse; Solomon Attaquin declares 'I want to see the day that I am a citizen and a man'
text: On February 9, 1869, Massachusetts State Senator Nathaniel Jay Holden and House Chairman Rodney French convened Wampanoag Tribe of Mashpee representatives in the Mashpee meetinghouse to discuss incorporating Mashpee as a township. Mashpee elder Solomon Attaquin told the legislative committee, 'I want to see the day that I am a citizen and a man,' while criticizing Governor Claflin's characterization of Mashpee non-proprietors.

headline: Mashpee and Gay Head incorporated as towns; guardianship era formally ends
text: In 1870, Mashpee and Gay Head were incorporated as towns, marking the official end of state-appointed guardianship. The Massachusetts Legislature authorized the sale of remaining tribally held Mashpee land and formally abolished the Mashpee district, establishing the town of Mashpee.

headline: Beulah Vanderhoop dies; her 70-year arc of activism (1811–1882) concludes
text: Beulah Vanderhoop (née Occouch), who had petitioned the Massachusetts legislature in 1811 and led petitioning efforts for decades, died in 1882. Her activism spanned from 1811 through the 1845 cranberry petition, making her a central figure in Mashpee and Gay Head's sustained resistance to colonial control over land and governance.

headline: Dawes Act passed, severing communal Indigenous land ownership through allotment
text: Congress passed the Dawes Act in 1887, severing communal Indigenous land ownership in Indian Territory by allotting lands to individuals rather than tribes, extending policies similar to those implemented in Massachusetts in 1869.

headline: Edwin DeVries Vanderhoop elected as representative to Massachusetts General Court from Dukes County
text: In 1888, Edwin DeVries Vanderhoop (married to Mary Cleggett) became the first Wampanoag man elected as a representative to the Massachusetts General Court on behalf of Dukes County.

headline: Mary Cleggett Vanderhoop publishes 'History of the Gay Head Indians'
text: Mary Cleggett Vanderhoop published 'The Gay Head Indians: Their History and Traditions' in the New Bedford Evening Standard in 1904, interrogating myths of European discovery of Martha's Vineyard and reclaiming Wampanoag history against narratives of disappearance.

headline: Netta Vanderhoop publishes 'The True Story of a Fugitive Slave' in Vineyard Gazette
text: The Vineyard Gazette published Netta Vanderhoop's account 'The True Story of a Fugitive Slave' on February 3, 1921, recounting her grandmother Beulah Vanderhoop's role in helping Edgar Jones escape slavery—a narrative that demonstrates long-standing Wampanoag participation in anti-slavery networks.

headline: Mashpee Tribe v. New Seabury Corp.: First Indian Nonintercourse Act jury trial
text: In 1977, the Mashpee Tribe's lawsuit against New Seabury Corporation, Mashpee v. New Seabury Corp., became the first litigation of the Indian Nonintercourse Act to go to a jury trial. In January 1978, the jury delivered its verdict finding that the Mashpee had been recognized as a tribe in the 1830s and 1840s but did not meet the legal definition of a tribe at other critical junctures, including when the lawsuit was filed.

headline: Mashpee Tribe v. Watt litigation continues
text: Following the 1977–1979 Mashpee v. New Seabury Corp. trial, the Mashpee Tribe pursued continued federal litigation in Mashpee Tribe v. Watt as part of sustained efforts to reclaim lands and assert sovereignty.

headline: Mashpee Tribe v. Secretary of Interior: Federal litigation ongoing
text: By 1989, the Mashpee Tribe's legal battles for federal recognition and land rights continued with Mashpee Tribe, et al. v. Secretary of the Interior, representing three decades of sustained petitioning and legal action—echoing the same strategies of collective advocacy that had characterized the 1811–1869 era.
